'''''Phedimus spurius''''', formerly '''''Sedum spurium''''', the '''Caucasian stonecrop''' or '''two-row stonecrop''', is a species of [[flowering plant]] in the family [[Crassulaceae]]. It is a low-growing, spreading [[succulent]] with stems that creep along the ground and root as they grow.

''P. spurius'' occurs naturally in the rocky subalpine meadows of [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]], [[northern Iran]], and northeastern [[Turkey]]. It has naturalized in Europe, often found along roadsides, walls, and waste areas, [[escaping cultivation]] to form persistent [[colony (biology)|colonies]]. It is widely grown for its tolerance of drought and rocky conditions. Wild populations and cultivars vary in color from white to red; greener-leaved plants produce paler blooms and those with red or purple foliage developing deeper-colored flowers.

==Taxonomy==
Species of ''[[Phedimus]]'' have traditionally been included in the genus ''[[Sedum]]''. Within the [[genus]] ''Phedimus'', ''P. spurius'' belongs to the [[subgenus]] ''Phedimus''.<ref name="Eggli"/> The [[specific epithet]], ''spurius'', means "false", though its intended meaning in this context is uncertain.<ref name="Missouri"/>
==Description==
''Phedimus spurius'' is a [[stonecrop]] with numerous stems that either sprawl along the ground or creep, often taking root as they grow. These stems, which are smooth or slightly bumpy, are typically 5–15 cm long. The leaves, which are usually arranged in opposite pairs but occasionally alternate, are either attached directly to the stem or have very short stalks.<ref name="Eggli"/> They grow in two rows along the stems, which is why the plant is sometimes called "two-row stonecrop",<ref name="Missouri"/> and vary in shape from spoon-like to rounded or oblong, with a wedge-shaped base and small, rounded teeth along the upper edges.<ref name="Eggli"/> Leaf size ranges from 15–35 mm in length and 10–12 mm in width.<ref name="Eggli">{{cite book | last=Eggli | first=Urs | title=Illustrated Handbook of Succulent Plants: Crassulaceae | publisher=Springer Berlin Heidelberg | year=2012 | isbn=978-3-642-55874-0 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=nU7mCAAAQBAJ&pg=PA201 | access-date=2 February 2025 | pages=197 (genus), 201–202 (species)}}</ref> The leaves are [[succulent]] and medium green with edges tinged in red. The older leaves (on the lower parts of the stems) are [[deciduous]], while the newer leaves (near the stem tips) are [[evergreen]]. In autumn, these upper leaves deepen to a rich burgundy color, persisting through winter.<ref name="Missouri"/>

[[File:Phedimus spurius 5.jpg|thumb|left|The flowers ''P. spurius'' may be white or red or any color in-between.]]

Flowering stems, which can lie along the ground or grow at an angle, reach 10–30 cm and have a rough texture<ref name="Eggli"/> and reddish color.<ref name="Missouri"/> The flowers are densely clustered in flat-topped groups called [[corymb]]s, each containing 15–30 blooms. The [[bracts]] (small, leaf-like structures beneath the flowers) are narrow and elongated. The flowers themselves usually have five, but occasionally six, [[petal]]s and sit on very short stalks or are nearly stalkless. The [[sepal]]s are triangular and pointed, sometimes with a slightly rough texture near the tip, growing up to 10 mm long. The petals are upright at the base but spread out towards the top, often with slightly curled tips and a central ridge. They measure 7–12 mm and come in shades from pure white to deep crimson. The flower's stamens are 5–9 mm long, with red pollen-producing structures.<ref name="Eggli"/> The species flowers from late spring to mid-summer, attracting butterflies.<ref name="Missouri"/> The small, four-sided nectar glands are about 0.5 × 1 mm. The fruit consists of five upright, smooth [[seed capsule]]s, each 5–9 mm long and joined at the base.<ref name="Eggli"/>

[[File:Растения в Седово 173.JPG|thumb|The size of the leaves of ''P. spurius'' is considerably variable among different populations.]]

''Phedimus spurius'' shows considerable [[variable species|variation]] in leaf shape and size, as well as flower color. In the northeastern part of its range, white-flowered forms (once described as ''Sedum involucratum'' and ''S. oppositifolium'') are more common, while in the west, red-flowered forms dominate. Despite these differences, genetic studies suggest that all forms belong to a single, uniform species.<ref name="Eggli"/> In early growth stages, ''P. spurius'' can resemble ''[[Phedimus hybridus|P. hybridus]]'' or ''[[Phedimus ellacombianus|P. ellacombianum]]'', but their differences become apparent upon flowering—while the latter two bear yellow blossoms, ''P. spurius'' does not. White-flowered varieties of ''P. spurius'' are generally less floriferous, yet all forms spread vigorously, with tangled stems extending beyond 30 cm over time—behavior uncommon in related species.<ref name="Stephenson"/>

==Distribution and habitat==
[[File:Phedimus spurius 423354700.jpg|thumb|White-flowered forms of ''P. spurius'' are more common in the northeast of its natural range.]]

The type specimen of ''Phedimus spurius'' was collected in [[Georgia (country)|Georgia]]. The species is distributed in Georgia, [[northern Iran]], and northeastern [[Turkey]], where it inhabits cool, rocky sites and [[subalpine meadow]]s at elevations ranging from 1,250 to 3,000 meters.<ref name="Eggli"/><ref name="Stephenson"/>

''Phedimus spurius'' has become [[naturalized species|naturalized]] in many parts of Europe,<ref name="Eggli"/> especially in various [[disturbed habitat]]s, such as walls, rocky areas, roadsides, refuse sites, and waste ground. It frequently [[escaped plant|escapes cultivation]], likely through [[garden waste]] disposal or [[dispersal by birds]].<ref name="q164"/> Once established, it can form persistent [[colony (biology)|colonies]].<ref name="q164">{{cite book | last1=Stroh | first1=P.A. | last2=Walker | first2=K.J. | last3=Humphrey | first3=T.A. | last4=Pescott | first4=O.L. | last5=Burkmar | first5=R.J. | title=Plant Atlas 2020: Mapping Changes in the Distribution of the British and Irish Flora | publisher=Princeton University Press | year=2023 | isbn=978-0-691-24760-1 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=xWqLEAAAQBAJ&pg=PA190 | access-date=2 February 2025 | page=190}}</ref>

==Cultivation==
The horticulturist Ray Stephenson has described ''Phedimus spurius'' as "perhaps ... the most common stonecrop in cultivation".<ref name="Stephenson">{{cite book | last=Stephenson | first=Ray | title=Sedum: Cultivated Stonecrops | publisher=Timber Press | year=1994 | isbn=978-1-60469-100-9 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=P5GGPwAACAAJ | access-date=2 February 2025 | page=143}}</ref> It thrives in well-drained, acidic to neutral soils with dry to moderate moisture levels and prefers full sun, though it can handle some light shade. It grows well in sandy or gravelly soil, adapts to nutrient-poor conditions, and requires proper drainage to stay healthy. It is highly [[drought-resistant]] and should not be overwatered. Pests and diseases rarely attack it, but snails, slugs, and [[scale insect]]s may appear.<ref name="Missouri"/>

''Phedimus spurius'' is commonly planted in [[rock garden]]s, small-scale [[ground cover]], and [[herbaceous border|border]] fronts, this plant also thrives in stone wall crevices, sunny slopes, and along edges.<ref name="Missouri"/> Due to its vigorous spreading habit, it is unsuitable for small rock gardens but excels as a fast-growing ground cover. It can overtake more delicate species and requires management. The plant struggles in containers, needing ample space to expand.<ref name="Stephenson"/> It may also be used in [[green roof]]s.<ref name="Rowe">{{cite journal | last1=Rowe | first1=D. Bradley | last2=Getter | first2=Kristin L. | last3=Durhman | first3=Angela K. | title=Effect of green roof media depth on Crassulacean plant succession over seven years | journal=Landscape and Urban Planning | publisher=Elsevier BV | volume=104 | issue=3–4 | year=2012 | issn=0169-2046 | doi=10.1016/j.landurbplan.2011.11.010 | pages=310–319| bibcode=2012LUrbP.104..310R }}</ref><ref name="Sutton">{{cite book | last=Sutton | first=Richard K. | title=Green Roof Ecosystems | publisher=Springer International Publishing | series=Ecological Studies | year=2015 | isbn=978-3-319-14983-7 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=zlHMCQAAQBAJ&pg=PA343 | access-date=3 February 2025 | pages=343–344}}</ref> It spreads easily by rooting at nodes that touch the ground and can be propagated effortlessly through cuttings or division.<ref name="Missouri">{{cite web | title=''Sedum spurium'' | website=Missouri Botanical Garden| url=https://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?taxonid=279381 | access-date=2 February 2025}}</ref>  Dark-leaved and variegated forms grow more slowly, making them valuable for contrast in borders.<ref name="Stephenson"/>

Numerous [[cultivars]] of ''Phedimus spurius'' have been developed, though many lack distinguishing traits. Leaf color correlates with flower shade—plants with the greenest foliage tend to produce the palest blooms, while those with wine-red, copper, or deep purple leaves develop progressively darker flowers.<ref name="Stephenson"/> The typical form has pink-purple flowers and green foliage that acquires a reddish hue in full sun. Cultivars vary in color intensity, from pale to dark.<ref name="Stephenson"/>

*'Coccineum' (syn. 'Splendens') is a cultivar with redder flowers and reddish-tinged foliage, cultivated for over a century.<ref name="Stephenson"/>
*'Album' (syn. ''Sedum oppositifolium'') is a white-flowered form with consistently green foliage, but reluctant to bloom.<ref name="Stephenson"/>
*'Green Mantle' (syn. 'Album Superbum') is similar to 'Album' but more floriferous, with white blooms that fade to pale pink.<ref name="Stephenson"/>
*'Salmoneum' is a North American selection with slightly more salmon-toned flowers than the typical species.<ref name="Stephenson"/>
*'Schorbuser Blut' ('Dragon's Blood'), a slow-growing yet highly sought-after form, begins the season with bright green, red-edged leaves but darkens by autumn.<ref name="Stephenson"/> It has received the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref name="RHS">{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/117391/Sedum-spurium-Schorbuser-Blut/Details | title = ''Sedum spurium'' 'Schorbuser Blut' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 5 March 2021}}</ref>
*'Roseum' is an older variety nearly identical to the species.<ref name="Stephenson"/>
*'Erd Blut' produces purple flowers with more deeply suffused foliage.<ref name="Stephenson"/>
<!---[[File:Sedum spurium Bronze Carpet.jpg|thumb|'Bronze Carpet' is a North American garden form.]]--->
*'Bronze Carpet' is a North American form with bronzed leaves and slightly deeper-colored flowers.<ref name="Stephenson"/>
<!---[[File:Sedum spurium Fuldaglut 1zz.jpg|thumb|'Fulda Glut' has reddish leaves and scarlet flowers.]]--->
*'Fulda Glut' is notably darker than the typical species. It also has reddish leaves but produces striking scarlet flowers.<ref name="RHS"/>
*''Sedum spurium'' 'Voodoo' has leaves heavily tinged with dark red and deep reddish-pink flowers.<ref name="RHS-Voodoo">{{cite web | title=Caucasian stonecrop 'Voodoo' Alpine Rockery/RHS | website=RHS | date=28 January 2025 | url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/211143/sedum-spurium-voodoo/details | access-date=3 February 2025}}</ref>
*'Ruby Mantle' features deep red foliage and purple blooms.<ref name="Stephenson"/>
*'Red Carpet' stands out with its bronze foliage and bright red blossoms.<ref name="RHS"/>
<!---[[File:Phedimus spurius 'Purpurteppich' kz01.jpg|thumb|'Purpurteppich' has brown-violet leaves in the spring.]]--->
*'Purpurteppich' ('Purple Carpet'), true to its name, bears purple flowers and large, springtime leaves that emerge brown-violet.<ref name="Stephenson"/>
*'Tricolor' is known in North America under this name, while in Europe it is sold as ''Sedum spurium'' var. ''variegatum''. Its leaves display a striking mix of green, creamy-white, and wine-red. The leaf shape differs from the species, leading to occasional misidentification as ''S. kamtschaticum'' var. ''variegatum''. However, the latter has a more upright habit and yellow flowers, whereas 'Tricolor' produces light pink-purple blooms. Reversion to solid green is common.<ref name="Stephenson"/>
*''Sedum spurium'' var. ''involucratum'' is rare in cultivation and identifiable by its exceptionally large sepals, nearly matching the petals in length. It is a small, light-petaled form with chromosome counts of 2n = 28 and 42.<ref name="Stephenson"/>
